title: Katt Williams Says He Outworked 300 Comedians to Build a Self-Funded Stand-Up Empire
text:

 Add preferred source Katt Williams, the stand-up comedian, tells The Diary of a CEO that his career rests on a measurable method — studying 300 working comedians, counting laughs against theirs, and betting only on himself. The interview traces a childhood of severe abuse, a departure from home at 13, and a business model built on self-financed specials licensed to networks for about a month before rights revert to him. Williams credits Prince for the ownership thesis and says early rejections were a gift because they preserved his independence. His advice to anyone building something: measure your output against peers, treat rejection as volume, and separate forgiveness from reconciliation. For investors and creators, the through-line is a case study in intellectual-property control and in the compounding advantage of treating your craft like a job with countable inputs. Key Elements 
 Katt Williams Steven Bartlett The Diary of a CEO HBO Comedy Central Prince Rogers Nelson Katt Williams Live Comic View Friday After Next According to Katt Katt Williams says his career was not built on talent. It was built on count — laughs, rejections, hours — and on a deliberate refusal to let anyone else own the things he made. Speaking to Steven Bartlett on The Diary of a CEO, the stand-up comedian laid out a working method that sounds less like inspiration and more like a sales playbook, then applied it to the thornier question of how a child raised in abuse decided he was worth betting on.
 The scale of the interview is the first clue that Williams is not improvising. He says he studied 300 working comedians, deliberately excluding the famous names, because "they were funnier than me and that's what I had to fix." He counted laughs per set. If a rival's fifteen minutes drew nine laughs, he aimed for sixteen or seventeen in the same window and did not cross the name off his list until he had outproduced them. He treated comedy as eight hours a day, seven days a week, "as a job because I expected a job's returns."
 That instinct came from door-to-door sales, which he entered around age sixteen and stuck with for roughly five years. His rule there was arithmetic: "it takes me 300 nos to get 30 yeses." The goal, he says, was to collect more rejections than the competition — not to avoid them. He tested the same principle earlier in landscaping, with one lawnmower and 26 clients, and in snow shoveling.
 The grind had a timetable, and Williams can recite it
 Bartlett structures the conversation around a hero's-journey arc, and Williams cooperates only partly — he resists the word "great" and says his aim was simply not to be mediocre. But he is precise about the sequence that took him from a five-minute club spot to his first special, a span of fifteen years.
 Stage What he did Duration / scale 
 First stand-up set Won a club competition after bluffing a bouncer; paid $25 for five minutes Age 16 
 Gap before returning Did not perform again because he did not see comedy as a job 5 years 
 Return to comedy Opened a tour as the five-minute act after winning a competition Age 20 
 Sacramento Moved to work white audiences and build a set that worked for any crowd 2 years 
 Oakland Moved to work Black audiences with a "high comedy IQ" 2.5 years 
 First milestone to first special From professional debut to Katt Williams Live 6 years to milestone; 15 years total to special 
 He says he moved to Los Angeles for 1999 into 2000 and that the plan worked in year one: Comic View , sitcom acting, and his first film audition, for Friday After Next , which he got. He attributes the speed to specific prayer rather than to strategy — a claim that recurs throughout the interview and sits uneasily beside his insistence that he authored every move.
 The specials were his, on Prince's advice
 The business model is the most transferable part of the conversation. Williams says he paid for his first special himself and "the next eight" after it. The mechanics he describes: shoot the special independently, license it to a network such as HBO or Comedy Central for a fee, let the license expire after about a month, then sell DVDs himself. Because the special was already shot, the license fee was profit on day one.
 His stated conclusion is a contrarian's version of gratitude: "I was so thankful that no one believed in me. I was so thankful that nobody wanted my product because it gave me the opportunity to have it."
 He credits the principle to Prince Rogers Nelson, whom he met before he had any entertainment job. Prince's argument, as Williams relays it: every artist starts 100% independent, then auctions off pieces of that independence to people who put up money. Williams's version of the lesson is to benchmark your worth against your peer group — a running back should know what running backs are paid — and to price accordingly. The risk is that when a creator gets hot, intermediaries arrive with short-term carrots that can shift incentives and strip away ownership. His defense is to know the comparable before you sit down.
 On risk itself, he draws a line between betting on things you control and things you do not. Wagering on a football game is risk; betting on himself is "zero risk," because he can decide to outwork, apologize, maneuver, or be vicious as the situation requires. He says he never had a plan B and never took a vacation in the lean years.
 "I only have one betting on myself and my God. I don't consider it a risk if what I'm betting on is myself."
 Seven years of beatings, and an exit staged by school staff
 The interview spends most of its 109 minutes on Williams's childhood, and Bartlett repeatedly tests the account against specifics — police photographs, the $1,200 he left with, the 35 arrests, the decision to self-finance. Williams is candid but declines to dwell; he describes himself as stoic on the subject and says he does not enjoy discussing himself.
 He says corporal punishment ran from age 5 to 12 and escalated from belts to extension cords to a water hose to a 2x4, and that he was tied to a pole in the basement for hours at a time. He describes being beaten unconscious and placed in an Epsom-salt bath before school so the bleeding would stop, and says he never missed a school day because school was his escape. He says both parents participated "evenly," and that he provoked some of it by questioning their Jehovah's Witness teachings — asking why the Bible, if divinely written, contained passages on how to treat slaves.
 He says he concluded early that his parents did not care for him as a person, and that his two younger brothers were treated differently: the middle brother resembled their father and "made the whole house better." Neither brother was tied up, he says. He describes his parents' marriage as outwardly the greatest love story he has known — still married, never seen them argue — which he calls "very confusing" against what happened behind the scenes.
 The exit was triggered by school administrators, not by him. He says he stopped dressing for gym, staff noticed, police were called, and photographs were taken of his back. The police told him they would arrest his parents the next day and remove all three children, but could not guarantee his brothers would stay together. He told his parents everything that evening, said he was leaving, and left with about $1,200. He was 13 and taller than his 5'3" father.
 "I'm not going to let you beat me again. That's where we are now."
 He rejects the word "runaway" and the word "homeless" for what followed. He took a truck to Florida because he did not want to face an Ohio winter alone, and slept in Peacock Park in Miami. He says the park's homeless community — professionals who had recently lost jobs, families, and homes to addiction — scared him off hard drugs permanently. He found off-the-books work and briefly tried car theft before stopping because he did not want that to be the thing he was good at.
 A year and a half later, a car pulled over
 Williams says that when he left, his parents moved the family to Florida the same day, so to relatives and fellow missionaries it looked like a family relocation rather than a child's disappearance. He had been checking milk-carton missing-person listings and concluded nobody was looking for him. Then, walking along a highway in Florida, a car pulled over: his parents and brothers. He describes no hug and no confrontation, and says his overwhelming feeling was joy at seeing his brothers, which erased whatever he expected to feel about his parents.
 He frames the episode as evidence of a larger pattern he calls non-coincidence: repeatedly, when he asked for something specific, an opportunity arrived from outside his own effort. He cites the Marine Corps rejection at 15 — he passed the tests but was four months too young — as the death of his stated childhood ambition, which was to be a soldier.
 God, separated from the religion that justified the abuse
 Williams wears a cross and speaks of an active, answering God, but says he is not religious and belongs to no religion. He drew the separation as a child: the religion was his parents' framework, and he says no religion condones beating a child unconscious, so the abuse was theirs, not the doctrine's. "I made a separation between religion and a relationship with God," he says. He has studied other religions and finds them largely agreeing on the goal — giving followers reasons to be better people and lines not to cross.
 He describes prayer as a negotiation with criteria: he asked for work that would let him be a single parent, be home during the day, work at night, and not require looking over his shoulder. He says the answer was comedy, and that he committed to repay it by working as hard as he could. He also says he asked to be delivered from himself, because he was disappointed to find he would entertain selling drugs for fast money.
 "I needed him to deliver me from me."
 His self-worth, he says, was never based on himself but on the God he serves — which is how he squares a childhood of being told he was unwanted with an adult who says he never doubted his worth. His advice to anyone who feels worthless is deliberately uncomfortable: "Your brain is not as smart as you think it is. Even if you have to lie to yourself about what your self-worth is, that's what you should do." Read more, he adds, because people with less talent and fewer opportunities have done what you are trying to do.
 Forgiveness without reconciliation
 Williams says he forgave his parents, that they never asked for it, and that forgiveness is something "you're allowed to do selfishly" because it helps the forgiver. He says he has stayed in contact and been available if they needed him, partly because they are now grandparents and he is a grandfather, but that his decision at 13 is the same as his decision at 55. Asked what they think of his success, he says: "I don't care, honestly." He adds that he did not think they should have been beating a celebrity — he thought they should not have been treating a kid like that.
 He is explicit that his story is not a template. He says no teenager could afford to leave home and hope for divine provision, and calls his own decisions "horrible." He says he tells the story so that a young reader understands that belief alone can carry someone, not so that anyone copies the exit.
 Time, attempts, and the story you are writing
 Williams's closing framework is that time is the only asset you control and that you can reset your life as many times as needed. He says the only regrets people report are things they did not try, and that the people who end up unhappy are those who never found their purpose — not those who chose a wrong path. He cites people who did nothing notable until 65 as proof that late starts are viable.
 He also describes using fiction as a decision tool. He read choose-your-own-adventure books, mapped best-case and worst-case outcomes before any move, and when genuinely stuck asked what a Black superhero would do and did that. He says he has deliberately preserved the five-year-old version of himself — curious, unwilling to believe something just because he heard it — and that his outward confidence has not changed since he was earning under $10,000 a year in stand-up.
 "Fear of failure should not be confused with confidence. I had an overwhelming fear of failure."
 He insists he has not been victimized, a stance that will strike some readers as implausible given the record he describes. "You can't do that and be winning all the time," he says. "And I'm literally winning all the time." It is less a denial of what happened than a refusal to let it become the organizing fact of his life.
 The unresolved tension is the one Williams names himself: he credits an unseen hand for pulling him out of each bad situation, yet also insists he authored every move and bet only on himself. Both claims sit in the same interview without reconciliation, and he seems to need both — the agency to justify the work, the providence to explain why a 13-year-old in Peacock Park is not the end of the story.
 For anyone building a business or a career out of a craft, the takeaway is more concrete than the biography. Williams's edge was not a secret technique; it was a spreadsheet mentality applied to a creative field — count the competitor's laughs, count your rejections, benchmark your rate against your peers, and keep the rights to what you make. The interview also flags what to watch: his podcast According to Katt , which he says is launching, and whether the memoir's account of the abuse draws any response from his parents, whom he says remain alive and in occasional contact.
